::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="k7-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Address</dt><dd>A column letter and a row number, such as B24; formulas point at addresses, not at numbers.</dd>
<dt>Relative address</dt><dd>B5 becomes B6 when filled down one row: right for data that changes row by row.</dd>
<dt>Absolute address</dt><dd>$E$1 never moves: right for one input, such as a price.</dd>
<dt>Range and function</dt><dd>SUM(F5:F28) adds every cell from F5 to F28; MAX, MIN and AVERAGE work the same way.</dd>
<dt>Check cell</dt><dd>A total computed two ways, which must agree: F30 against E30 × E2. Agreement shows the sheet is consistent, not that its inputs are right.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The same column in Python</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A spreadsheet column with one formula filled down is what a data table calls a vectorised operation: one line acts on every row at once. With the day in a pandas table `df` and the inputs as plain variables:

```python
nuclear = 100                                              # E1: MW, runs flat
gas_cost = 40                                              # E2: $/MWh
df["gas_mw"] = df["demand"] - df["wind"] - df["solar"] - nuclear
df["gas_cost"] = df["gas_mw"] * 1 * gas_cost               # MW × 1 h × $/MWh
df["gas_cost"].sum(), df["gas_mw"].max()                   # F30 and E31
```

No addresses and no fill-down, so no sliding E1. Bridge B2 does this with a whole year of real hourly data.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>When to leave the spreadsheet</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Size: a year of hours is 8,760 rows per column; many plants or regions multiply that quickly.</li>
<li>Checking: a formula hidden in one cell is easy to break and hard to review; code can be read, tested and versioned (toolbox <a href="k08-git-notebooks.html">K8</a>).</li>
<li>Optimization: a sheet computes what a plan costs; choosing the best plan needs a solver (bridge B1).</li>
<li>Still useful: quick estimates, a check of a model's totals, and tables to share. Many studies keep a sheet for exactly that.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="k7-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="typed" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Typing 120 into E5 is as good as the formula, as long as the number is right.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A typed number does not follow its inputs: change the demand or the nuclear output and E5 silently goes wrong.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dollar" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “=E5*$E$2 filled down to row 6 becomes =E6*$E$2.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. E5 is relative and moves one row; $E$2 is absolute and stays.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="k7">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mixed" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A formula in B10 reads =B5*$A10. Filled right to C10, it becomes…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">=B5*$A10</li><li data-value="b">=C5*$A10</li><li data-value="c">=C5*$B10</li><li data-value="d">=B5*$B10</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>=C5*$A10: B5 moves one column; $A10 has its column fixed, so it stays in column A.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="units" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Each row is one hour. What unit does =SUM(E5:E28) have, if column E is in MW?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">MW</li><li data-value="b">MW per hour</li><li data-value="c">MWh, because each row lasts 1 h</li><li data-value="d">$</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>MWh: each row's MW lasts one hour, so each adds MW × 1 h. With 15-minute rows you would multiply the sum by 0.25 h.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="k7-practice">
<!-- k7-practice:start (written by _tests/learn/test_k07-spreadsheets.js in its write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card k7-practice"><div class="lx-x-head"><h3>Practice sheet</h3></div>
<p class="lx-hint">Use the table of the day above. With JavaScript on, you type each answer as a formula in a working sheet (about 30 minutes).</p><ol class="k7-tasks">
<li>Total demand energy over the day, in MWh (each row is one hour). <details class="k7-hint"><summary>Answer</summary><code>=SUM(B5:B28)</code> = 6,957 MWh</details></li>
<li>Share of the day's demand met by wind and solar, in %. <details class="k7-hint"><summary>Answer</summary><code>=SUM(C5:D28)/SUM(B5:B28)*100</code> = 37.3%</details></li>
<li>Average gas need over the five hourly rows labelled 17:00 to 21:00, in MW. <details class="k7-hint"><summary>Answer</summary><code>=AVERAGE(E22:E26)</code> = 112 MW</details></li>
<li>The day's highest solar output, in MW. <details class="k7-hint"><summary>Answer</summary><code>=MAX(D5:D28)</code> = 161 MW</details></li>
<li>The day's gas cost if gas cost $55 per MWh, without changing E2. <details class="k7-hint"><summary>Answer</summary><code>=E30*55</code> = $108,075</details></li>
</ol></div>
<!-- k7-practice:end -->
</div>
```
